glossary.definition: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: the security rules for any business that stores, processes or transmits payment card data.
Cardholder data environment: the people, processes and systems that handle card data, and anything connected to them.
Primary account number: the long number on a payment card.
Sensitive authentication data, such as the full magnetic-stripe data, card verification code and PINs, which must never be kept after authorization.
Third-party service provider: an outside company that handles card data or can affect its security on the entity's behalf.
Network security control, such as a firewall or other device or service that controls traffic between networks.
Multi-factor authentication: signing in with two or more independent factors.
Qualified Security Assessor: an assessor certified by the PCI Security Standards Council.
Report on Compliance: the formal assessment report a QSA completes.
Self-Assessment Questionnaire: the self-assessment form for smaller merchants and service providers.

families.name: Install and Maintain Network Security Controls

controls.title: Network security policies maintained and known
controls.description: The organization keeps written policies and operating procedures for its firewalls and other NSCs, keeps them current, and makes sure the people who rely on them actually use them. Without this, network protections depend on memory and drift over time.
controls.guidance: Request the network security policy and procedure documents and confirm they carry a recent review date. Interview network staff to confirm they know where the documents live and follow them day to day.

controls.title: Network security duties assigned and understood
controls.description: Someone is named as responsible for each network security activity, and those people know and accept what is expected of them. Clear ownership stops tasks from falling between teams.
controls.guidance: Look for a RACI chart, job descriptions or a responsibility matrix covering Requirement 1 tasks. Interview the named owners to confirm they understand their duties.

controls.title: NSC configuration standards defined and applied
controls.description: There are written standards for how NSC rulesets must be built, and every NSC is configured and kept in line with them. Consistent standards make misconfigured or overly open rules far less likely.
controls.guidance: Review the NSC configuration standards, then compare a sample of live firewall, router and cloud security group configurations against them. Confirm the standards have been reviewed and kept up to date.

controls.title: Network changes go through change control
controls.description: Any change to network connections or NSC settings is requested, approved, tested where needed and recorded through the organization's formal change process. This prevents unreviewed changes from quietly opening paths into the CDE.
controls.guidance: Pick a sample of recent firewall or network changes and trace each to an approved change ticket with documented testing and sign-off. Confirm that what was approved matches what was implemented.

controls.title: Network diagram kept current
controls.description: An up-to-date diagram shows how the CDE connects to every other network, including wireless segments. Knowing exactly where connections exist is the starting point for protecting them.
controls.guidance: Obtain the network diagram, check its revision date, and walk through it with network staff. Spot check a few connections against actual configurations to confirm the diagram reflects reality.

controls.title: Cardholder data flow diagram kept current
controls.description: A diagram traces where account data travels across systems and networks, and it is refreshed whenever the environment changes. This makes it possible to see every place that card data must be protected.
controls.guidance: Review the data flow diagram and compare it with interviews and observed payment flows. Confirm it is updated after significant changes and covers all channels that handle account data.

controls.title: Allowed ports, protocols and services approved
controls.description: Every port, protocol and service permitted through the network is listed, has a business reason, and has been formally approved. Anything not on the list should not be allowed.
controls.guidance: Request the approved list of ports, protocols and services with business justifications and approver names. Compare it with a sample of NSC rulesets to confirm nothing extra is permitted.

controls.title: Risky services protected by extra controls
controls.description: Where the organization has decided to keep a service or protocol that is known to be insecure, it puts specific safeguards in place to reduce the risk. Leaving weak protocols unguarded invites easy compromise.
controls.guidance: Identify any insecure services from the approved list, then check the documented compensating safeguards and verify them in configuration. Interview staff about how those protections are maintained.

controls.title: NSC rules reviewed at least every six months
controls.description: Firewall and other NSC configurations are reviewed at least twice a year to confirm every rule is still needed and correct. Regular review removes stale or overly broad rules before they become a problem.
controls.guidance: Ask for records of the last two NSC rule reviews, including who performed them and what was changed or removed. Confirm the reviews were no more than six months apart.

controls.title: NSC configuration files secured and in sync
controls.description: Stored NSC configuration files are protected from unauthorized access and match what is actually running, so a device restart or restore does not load outdated or insecure rules.
controls.guidance: Check access permissions on stored configuration and backup files. Compare a sample of saved configurations with the running configurations to confirm they match.

controls.title: Inbound traffic to the CDE limited
controls.description: Traffic coming into the CDE is restricted to what is strictly needed, and all other inbound traffic is explicitly denied. This shrinks the ways an attacker could reach card data.
controls.guidance: Review NSC rules governing traffic into the CDE and confirm each allowed flow has a business reason. Verify a deny-all rule or equivalent default blocks everything else.

controls.title: Outbound traffic from the CDE limited
controls.description: Traffic leaving the CDE is limited to what the business requires, with all other outbound connections blocked. This makes it harder for stolen data to be sent out or for malware to call home.
controls.guidance: Examine egress rules for the CDE and confirm each permitted destination is justified. Check that a default deny applies to all other outbound traffic.

controls.title: Wireless networks separated from the CDE
controls.description: NSCs sit between any wireless network and the CDE, so wireless traffic is blocked by default and only authorized, necessary traffic reaches card data systems. Wireless networks are easy targets and must not offer a shortcut in.
controls.guidance: Use the network diagram to locate all wireless networks and inspect the NSCs separating them from the CDE. Confirm a default deny applies and any allowed traffic is approved.

controls.title: NSCs between trusted and untrusted networks
controls.description: Firewalls or equivalent controls are placed at every boundary between internal networks and untrusted ones such as the internet. These boundaries are the first line of defense against outside attackers.
controls.guidance: Compare the network diagram with deployed devices to confirm an NSC exists at each connection to an untrusted network. Review the configurations of those devices.

controls.title: Untrusted inbound traffic tightly restricted
controls.description: Traffic from untrusted networks into trusted ones is only allowed when it reaches public-facing services on approved ports, or when it is a reply to a connection started from inside. Everything else is blocked.
controls.guidance: Review internet-facing NSC rules to confirm inbound access is limited to approved public services and stateful return traffic. Look for any rule that allows broad inbound access.

controls.title: Spoofed traffic blocked at the perimeter
controls.description: Perimeter controls detect and drop traffic pretending to come from an internal address, so attackers cannot disguise malicious packets as trusted traffic.
controls.guidance: Inspect perimeter device configurations for anti-spoofing settings, such as filtering of internal or private source addresses arriving from outside.

controls.title: Card data stores not reachable from untrusted networks
controls.description: Systems that hold cardholder data cannot be reached directly from the internet or other untrusted networks. Keeping storage behind internal layers adds a barrier attackers must cross.
controls.guidance: Identify systems storing cardholder data from the data flow diagram and confirm by configuration review that no direct path exists to them from untrusted networks.

controls.title: Internal IP addresses and routes kept private
controls.description: Internal IP addresses and routing details are only revealed to parties who are authorized to know them. Hiding this information makes it harder for attackers to map the network.
controls.guidance: Check for techniques such as NAT, proxies or filtered route advertisements. Review how internal addressing information is shared externally and confirm it is limited to authorized parties.

controls.title: Dual-connected devices protected
controls.description: Laptops and other devices, including employee-owned ones, that join the CDE and also go online through untrusted networks have security controls active so they cannot carry threats inside. Users cannot switch those controls off unless specifically approved for a limited time.
controls.guidance: Review the policy for such devices and inspect a sample to confirm personal firewalls or equivalent controls are running and locked against user changes. Check records of any approved temporary exceptions.

families.name: Apply Secure Configurations to All System Components

controls.title: Secure configuration policies maintained and known
controls.description: Written policies and procedures cover how systems are securely configured, are kept up to date, and are known and used by the staff who apply them. This keeps hardening consistent across the environment.
controls.guidance: Request the configuration policy and procedure documents and confirm a recent review date. Interview administrators to confirm they know and follow the documents.

controls.title: Secure configuration duties assigned and understood
controls.description: Responsibility for each secure configuration activity is assigned to named people who understand their role. Clear ownership makes sure hardening tasks actually get done.
controls.guidance: Look for a responsibility matrix or job descriptions covering Requirement 2 tasks, and interview the assigned personnel to confirm awareness.

controls.title: Hardening standards cover all system types
controls.description: The organization keeps configuration standards for every type of system component, based on recognized hardening guidance, that address known weaknesses. The standards are refreshed as new vulnerabilities appear and are applied whenever new systems are built.
controls.guidance: Review the configuration standards and confirm they reference industry hardening sources such as CIS Benchmarks. Check that they cover all component types in scope and are applied to a sample of newly deployed systems.

controls.title: Vendor default accounts disabled or changed
controls.description: Built-in vendor accounts are either removed or disabled, or their default passwords are changed before use. Default credentials are widely published and are one of the easiest ways in.
controls.guidance: Inspect a sample of systems, applications and devices for active vendor default accounts and attempt or review evidence of changed passwords. Interview staff about the process used during deployment.

controls.title: Separate functions with different security needs
controls.description: Functions that need different levels of protection are kept apart, for example on separate servers or virtual machines, or are all secured to the highest level required. This stops a weaker function from exposing a more sensitive one.
controls.guidance: Review a sample of system components to see what functions each one runs. Where mixed functions share a system, confirm they are all secured to the strictest standard needed.

controls.title: Unnecessary services and functions removed
controls.description: Only the services, protocols, software and features a system genuinely needs are enabled; everything else is removed or turned off. Fewer running components means fewer ways to attack.
controls.guidance: Compare enabled services and installed software on a sample of systems against the configuration standards. Ask for justification of anything that appears unnecessary.

controls.title: Insecure services justified and protected
controls.description: If any insecure protocol or service is kept running, the business reason is documented and extra protections are applied to reduce the risk it creates.
controls.guidance: Identify insecure services on sampled systems, review the documented justification, and verify the additional safeguards are configured.

controls.title: Security settings configured to prevent misuse
controls.description: Security parameters on each system are set to stop misuse, following the organization's configuration standards. Poorly tuned settings can undo otherwise good hardening.
controls.guidance: Inspect security parameters on a sample of operating systems, databases and applications and compare them with the documented standards. Interview administrators on how settings are maintained.

controls.title: Admin access over the network encrypted
controls.description: All administrative access that does not happen at the physical console is protected with strong cryptography, so admin credentials and commands cannot be intercepted.
controls.guidance: Observe administrators connecting remotely and check that protocols such as SSH or TLS are used. Review configurations to confirm cleartext admin protocols such as Telnet are disabled.

controls.title: Wireless defaults changed before use
controls.description: Wireless networks that connect to the CDE or carry account data have all vendor defaults changed when installed or confirmed secure, including encryption keys, admin passwords, SNMP strings and similar settings. Factory wireless settings are well known to attackers.
controls.guidance: Review wireless setup procedures and inspect access point configurations for default SSIDs, passwords, SNMP community strings and keys. Interview staff responsible for wireless deployment.

controls.title: Wireless keys rotated after staff leave or compromise
controls.description: Encryption keys for in-scope wireless networks are replaced when someone who knew them leaves, and whenever a key may have been exposed. Old keys in former employees' hands are a lasting risk.
controls.guidance: Review the key change procedure and compare records of wireless key changes with staff departure records and any suspected compromise events.

controls.title: Data protection policies maintained and known
controls.description: Policies and procedures for protecting stored account data are written down, kept current, and known and used by relevant staff. Clear direction keeps data handling consistent.
controls.guidance: Request the stored data protection policies and procedures, confirm a recent review date, and interview staff to confirm they follow them.

controls.title: Data protection duties assigned and understood
controls.description: Named people are responsible for each activity involved in protecting stored account data, and they understand those responsibilities.
controls.guidance: Look for documented assignments covering Requirement 3 tasks, and interview the responsible personnel.

controls.title: Card data retention kept to a minimum
controls.description: Account data is kept only as long as there is a legal, regulatory or business need, under defined retention rules, and is securely deleted afterward. This includes any sensitive authentication data held before a transaction is authorized. Less stored data means less to lose.
controls.guidance: Review the retention and disposal policy and confirm it defines what is kept, why and for how long. Sample data stores to verify data older than the defined period has been removed, and check records of the periodic disposal process.

controls.title: No SAD kept after authorization
controls.description: Sensitive authentication data is never retained once a transaction has been authorized, even if it was encrypted. If this data is stolen it can be used to create counterfeit cards or fraudulent transactions.
controls.guidance: Review data flows and inspect databases, logs, files and debug output on a sample of systems for SAD. Interview staff about how SAD is purged after authorization.

controls.title: Full magnetic stripe data not retained
controls.description: The complete contents of any card track, whether from the magnetic stripe or the chip equivalent, are not stored after a transaction is authorized.
controls.guidance: Search sampled data sources such as transaction logs, history files and database schemas for full track data, and confirm none is present after authorization.

controls.title: Card verification codes not retained
controls.description: The three or four digit security code printed on the card is not stored once the transaction is authorized.
controls.guidance: Inspect sampled data stores, logs and input forms for stored card verification codes, and confirm they are discarded after authorization.

controls.title: PINs and PIN blocks not retained
controls.description: The cardholder's PIN and any encrypted PIN block are not stored after authorization.
controls.guidance: Examine sampled data stores and logs for PIN or PIN block values, and confirm none remain after authorization.

controls.title: Pre-authorization SAD encrypted
controls.description: If sensitive authentication data must be held electronically before a transaction is authorized, it is protected with strong cryptography while it is stored.
controls.guidance: Identify where SAD is held before authorization and review the encryption method and configuration protecting it.

controls.title: Issuer SAD storage justified and secured
controls.description: Card issuers, and companies supporting issuing services, store sensitive authentication data only where there is a documented, legitimate issuing need, and protect it with strong cryptography.
controls.guidance: Review the documented business justification for SAD storage and examine where and how it is stored, including the encryption in use.

controls.title: PAN masked on screen by default
controls.description: When a PAN is displayed, it is masked so that no more than the first six and last four digits show, and only people with a documented business need can see more. Masking limits exposure to anyone looking at screens, reports or receipts.
controls.guidance: Review the list of roles allowed to see more of the PAN, then observe displays, reports and receipts for both privileged and standard users to confirm masking works as documented.

controls.title: Remote access blocks copying of PAN
controls.description: When people use remote-access tools, they are technically prevented from copying or moving PAN to other locations unless they are explicitly authorized with a documented business need. This keeps card data from leaking onto unmanaged machines.
controls.guidance: Review remote-access tool configurations for controls such as disabled clipboard, file transfer and local drive mapping. Check the list of users approved for exceptions and their justification.

controls.title: Stored PAN rendered unreadable
controls.description: Wherever PAN is stored, including backups and logs, it is made unreadable using an accepted method such as strong one-way hashing of the full PAN, truncation, index tokens, or strong encryption with managed keys. This protects the data even if storage is breached.
controls.guidance: Review documentation of the method used, then inspect sampled data repositories, removable media and audit logs to confirm PAN is not stored in readable form.

controls.title: PAN hashes use keyed cryptography
controls.description: When hashing is used to protect PAN, the hash must be a keyed cryptographic hash of the full PAN, with the keys managed properly. Plain unkeyed hashes of card numbers can be reversed by trying every possible value.
controls.guidance: Review the hashing design and configuration to confirm a keyed algorithm such as HMAC is used, and check that associated keys follow the key management procedures.

controls.title: Disk encryption limited to removable media
controls.description: Disk or partition-level encryption is only accepted as the way of protecting PAN on removable media. On other systems, PAN must also be protected by another method that meets the core requirement for making it unreadable.
controls.guidance: Identify where disk-level encryption is relied on. For non-removable storage, confirm an additional method such as field encryption, truncation or tokens protects the PAN.

controls.title: Disk encryption access managed independently
controls.description: Where disk-level encryption protects PAN, logical access to it is controlled separately from the operating system login, and decryption keys are not tied to user accounts. Otherwise anyone who logs in would see the data in the clear.
controls.guidance: Examine the disk encryption configuration and authentication process to confirm it uses its own access mechanism. Check where decryption keys are stored and that they are not linked to user accounts.

controls.title: Procedures protect encryption keys from misuse
controls.description: Documented procedures protect the keys that secure stored account data against disclosure and misuse. They cover limiting access to the fewest custodians, making key-encrypting keys at least as strong as the keys they protect, keeping key types apart, and storing keys securely in the fewest places.
controls.guidance: Review key management procedures for coverage of these protections. Interview key custodians and inspect key storage to confirm the procedures are followed.

controls.title: Cryptographic architecture documented
controls.description: Service providers keep a current description of their cryptographic architecture, covering algorithms, protocols, key strengths, cryptoperiods, how each key is used, and the HSMs or secure devices involved. This helps them avoid reusing production keys in test and lets them react quickly when an algorithm is weakened.
controls.guidance: Request the cryptographic architecture document and check it lists algorithms, key strengths, expiry dates, key usage, and an inventory of HSMs or secure cryptographic devices. Interview staff to confirm it reflects the current environment.

controls.title: Secret and private keys stored securely
controls.description: Secret and private keys that protect stored account data are only kept in approved forms: encrypted under a key-encrypting key, inside a secure cryptographic device such as an HSM, or as split components or key shares.
controls.guidance: Review key storage documentation and inspect where keys are held to confirm they exist only in one of the approved protected forms, never as a single cleartext key.

controls.title: Cleartext key component access tightly limited
controls.description: Access to any key components in cleartext form is restricted to as few custodians as practical. Fewer people with access means less chance of a key being misused.
controls.guidance: Review the list of custodians with access to cleartext key components and compare it with access controls and logs. Confirm each person has a defined need.

controls.title: Keys held in as few places as possible
controls.description: Cryptographic keys are stored in the smallest number of locations needed. Every extra copy is another place an attacker could find a key.
controls.guidance: Review key inventory and storage locations and interview custodians to confirm keys are not duplicated beyond what operations require.

controls.title: Strong key generation procedures
controls.description: Procedures ensure that keys protecting stored account data are generated in a way that makes them strong and unpredictable.
controls.guidance: Review key generation procedures and observe or examine evidence of how keys are created, such as the use of an approved random number generator or HSM.

controls.title: Secure key distribution procedures
controls.description: Procedures ensure that keys are delivered only to authorized recipients and are protected throughout the distribution process.
controls.guidance: Review key distribution procedures and examine records of recent key transfers to confirm protected methods and authorized recipients.

controls.title: Secure key storage procedures
controls.description: Procedures define how keys protecting stored account data are kept safe while at rest, so they cannot be read or tampered with.
controls.guidance: Review key storage procedures and inspect key storage mechanisms to confirm keys are protected as described.

controls.title: Keys changed at the end of their cryptoperiod
controls.description: Keys are replaced when their defined lifetime ends, based on the cryptoperiod set by the organization in line with industry guidance. Limiting how long a key is used reduces the damage if it is ever exposed.
controls.guidance: Review defined cryptoperiods for each key type and check key change records to confirm keys were rotated on schedule.

controls.title: Weak or compromised keys retired
controls.description: Keys are retired, replaced or destroyed when they reach the end of their life, when their integrity is in doubt, when a custodian with knowledge of a cleartext component leaves, or when compromise is suspected. Retired keys kept for archive are never used for live encryption.
controls.guidance: Review procedures for key retirement and replacement and examine records of retired keys. Confirm any archived keys are used only for decryption or verification.

controls.title: Split knowledge for manual key handling
controls.description: When keys are managed manually in cleartext, no single person can know or control the whole key; at least two people each hold separate parts. This prevents one individual from misusing a key on their own.
controls.guidance: Review manual key management procedures and observe or interview custodians to confirm key components are held by different people and that two people are needed for each operation.

controls.title: Unauthorized key substitution prevented
controls.description: Procedures and controls stop anyone from swapping in an unauthorized key in place of a legitimate one.
controls.guidance: Review procedures and system controls that authenticate keys before use, and interview custodians about how substitution is detected and prevented.

controls.title: Key custodians formally accept their duties
controls.description: Each key custodian signs off, on paper or electronically, confirming they know and accept what their key management role requires.
controls.guidance: Request signed or electronic acknowledgment forms for all current key custodians and compare them with the custodian list.

controls.title: Key handling guidance shared with customers
controls.description: Service providers that share keys with customers for sending or storing account data give those customers documented guidance on securely transmitting, storing and updating the keys.
controls.guidance: Review the documentation the service provider supplies to customers and confirm it covers secure transmission, storage and update of shared keys.

families.name: Protect Cardholder Data with Strong Cryptography During Transmission Over Open, Public Networks

controls.title: Transmission security policies maintained and known
controls.description: Policies and procedures for protecting card data in transit are documented, kept current, and known and used by relevant staff.
controls.guidance: Request the transmission security policies and procedures, check their review date, and interview staff to confirm they follow them.

controls.title: Transmission security duties assigned and understood
controls.description: Named people are responsible for each activity in protecting card data during transmission, and they understand those responsibilities.
controls.guidance: Look for documented assignments covering Requirement 4 tasks, and interview the responsible personnel.

controls.title: Strong encryption for PAN over public networks
controls.description: PAN sent over open, public networks such as the internet is protected with strong cryptography and secure protocols, using only trusted, valid certificates that have not expired or been revoked. Insecure protocol versions and weak settings are not allowed, and encryption strength matches the method used.
controls.guidance: Review transmission configurations, such as TLS settings on web servers and APIs, to confirm modern protocol versions and strong cipher suites. Check that certificates are valid, unexpired and issued by trusted authorities, and observe sample transmissions where practical.

controls.title: Inventory of trusted keys and certificates
controls.description: The organization keeps an up-to-date list of the keys and certificates it trusts for protecting PAN in transit. Tracking them prevents surprise expirations and helps spot rogue or outdated certificates.
controls.guidance: Request the key and certificate inventory and compare a sample of certificates in use against it. Confirm the inventory records details such as owner and expiry date and is kept current.

controls.title: Wireless links carrying PAN use strong encryption
controls.description: Wireless networks that carry PAN or connect to the CDE use industry best practices for authentication and encryption, so card data cannot be intercepted over the air.
controls.guidance: Inspect wireless network configurations for modern authentication and encryption settings, such as WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise, and confirm deprecated options are disabled.

controls.title: PAN protected in end-user messaging
controls.description: Whenever PAN is sent through end-user messaging such as email, chat or text messages, it is protected with strong cryptography. These channels are easy to intercept and are not secure on their own.
controls.guidance: Review policies on sending PAN through messaging tools and examine the configuration of any tools used for it to confirm encryption is applied. Interview staff about how they handle requests to send card numbers.

families.name: Protect All Systems and Networks from Malicious Software

controls.title: Malware protection policies documented and in use
controls.description: The organization keeps written security policies and operating procedures for defending against malicious software, keeps them current, and makes sure the people who rely on them know them. Clear, shared rules mean malware defenses are run the same way every time.
controls.guidance: Review the malware protection policies and procedures for currency and approval. Interview staff with anti-malware duties to confirm they know where the documents live and follow them day to day.

controls.title: Malware protection roles assigned and understood
controls.description: Each task in the malware protection program has a named owner, and those owners know what they are accountable for. Without clear ownership, updates, alerts and exceptions can fall through the cracks.
controls.guidance: Look for a RACI chart, job descriptions or similar records that assign anti-malware duties. Interview the people named to confirm they understand and accept their responsibilities.

controls.title: Anti-malware installed on in-scope systems
controls.description: Every in-scope system runs an anti-malware tool, unless a documented assessment shows that type of system is not exposed to malware. Unprotected machines give attackers an easy foothold in the environment.
controls.guidance: Compare the system inventory against the anti-malware console to confirm coverage. For any system without protection, ask for the written assessment that justifies the exclusion.

controls.title: Anti-malware handles all known malware types
controls.description: The chosen anti-malware tooling can find known kinds of malicious software and then remove it, block it, or isolate it. A tool that only alerts without stopping the threat leaves systems exposed.
controls.guidance: Review vendor documentation and the product configuration to see which malware categories are covered. Confirm that removal, blocking or quarantine actions are enabled, not just detection.

controls.title: Low-risk systems reviewed for malware exposure
controls.description: Systems excluded from anti-malware because they are considered low risk are listed and reassessed on a regular schedule. Threats change over time, so a platform that was once safe may later need protection.
controls.guidance: Request the list of excluded system types and the most recent periodic evaluations. Check that each review considered current threats and reached a documented conclusion.

controls.title: Review frequency for low-risk systems set by risk
controls.description: How often the organization reassesses systems excluded from anti-malware is decided through a targeted risk analysis. Setting the interval based on actual risk keeps the review cadence defensible.
controls.guidance: Obtain the targeted risk analysis that sets the review interval. Confirm the reviews of excluded systems are happening at the frequency it specifies.

controls.title: Anti-malware signatures and engines kept current
controls.description: Anti-malware software and its detection definitions update automatically so they recognize the latest threats. Outdated definitions miss new malware that attackers are actively using.
controls.guidance: Inspect the anti-malware console settings to confirm automatic updates are on. Sample endpoints and servers to verify their definition versions are recent.

controls.title: Ongoing malware scanning or behavior analysis
controls.description: Anti-malware either runs scheduled and real-time scans, or watches system behavior continuously to spot threats. One of these approaches must be active so malware is caught soon after it arrives.
controls.guidance: Review the anti-malware policy configuration for scan schedules, on-access scanning or behavioral monitoring. Check logs from sampled systems to confirm scans or monitoring are actually running.

controls.title: Malware scan schedule set by risk analysis
controls.description: Where the organization relies on periodic malware scans, it decides how often to run them through a targeted risk analysis. This links scanning frequency to the real level of exposure.
controls.guidance: Obtain the targeted risk analysis that sets the scan interval. Compare it with scan configurations and logs to confirm scans run as often as the analysis requires.

controls.title: Removable media scanned for malware
controls.description: USB drives and other removable media are scanned automatically when plugged in, or are monitored continuously while connected. Portable storage is a common way for malware to bypass network defenses.
controls.guidance: Review anti-malware settings for removable media scanning or behavioral monitoring. Test on a sample system, or review logs, to confirm the scan triggers when media is inserted.

controls.title: Anti-malware logs enabled and retained
controls.description: Anti-malware tools produce audit logs, and those logs are kept in line with the organization's log retention rules. These records help investigators trace how an infection started and spread.
controls.guidance: Inspect anti-malware configuration to confirm logging is on and forwarded to central storage. Check that retained logs go back as far as the retention policy requires.

controls.title: Users cannot disable anti-malware
controls.description: Ordinary users are prevented from turning off or changing anti-malware protection. Any temporary exception requires management approval for a specific case and a limited time.
controls.guidance: Review endpoint policy settings that lock the agent against user changes. Try to disable it on a sample machine and review records of any approved temporary exceptions.

controls.title: Anti-phishing protection in place
controls.description: The organization uses technical controls, such as email filtering and link scanning, to detect phishing messages and protect staff from them. Phishing is one of the most common ways attackers steal credentials.
controls.guidance: Review email security gateway and anti-phishing tool configurations, for example DMARC, SPF, DKIM and link or attachment scanning. Ask for reports that show phishing messages being caught.

families.name: Develop and Maintain Secure Systems and Software

controls.title: Secure development policies documented and in use
controls.description: Written policies and procedures cover how systems and software are built and maintained securely. They are kept up to date and known by the teams who need them, so secure practices are applied consistently.
controls.guidance: Review the secure development and maintenance policies for currency and approval. Interview developers and system administrators to confirm they know and follow them.

controls.title: Secure development roles assigned and understood
controls.description: Responsibilities for secure system and software work are assigned to specific people, who know what they own. Clear accountability keeps security tasks from being skipped during busy delivery cycles.
controls.guidance: Look for documented assignments such as a RACI matrix or role descriptions. Interview the assigned staff to confirm they understand their duties.

controls.title: Custom software built using secure practices
controls.description: Software the organization writes itself, or has written for it, follows recognized secure coding practices and builds in security across every stage of development. Security designed in from the start costs less than fixing flaws later.
controls.guidance: Review the software development lifecycle documentation and the industry standards it references. Check a sample of projects for evidence that security activities happened at each phase.

controls.title: Annual secure coding training for developers
controls.description: Staff who build custom software receive secure coding training at least once a year, covering the languages and tools they use and how to spot common vulnerabilities. Trained developers write fewer exploitable flaws.
controls.guidance: Obtain training records for the development team and confirm each person completed training in the last twelve months. Review course content to see it fits the team's technology stack.

controls.title: Code reviewed before release to production
controls.description: Custom code is checked for security problems before it goes live, either by people or by automated tools. Reviews confirm secure practices were followed and catch flaws before customers or attackers find them.
controls.guidance: Review the code review procedure and sample recent releases for evidence of completed reviews, such as pull request approvals or scan reports. Confirm issues found were fixed before deployment.

controls.title: Manual code reviews are independent and approved
controls.description: When code is reviewed by hand, the reviewer is someone other than the author and knows secure coding. Management approves the results before release, which keeps reviews objective.
controls.guidance: Sample manual code reviews and check that the reviewer was not the author and has relevant expertise. Look for documented management sign-off before each change was released.

controls.title: Development defends against common attack types
controls.description: Developers use proven coding techniques to stop well-known attacks, including injection, unsafe data handling, broken access control and cross-site scripting. These flaws are among the most frequently exploited in payment applications.
controls.guidance: Review coding standards for the techniques used against each common attack category. Interview developers and look at code samples or test results showing those techniques in use.

controls.title: Vulnerabilities tracked and risk-ranked
controls.description: The organization watches trusted sources for newly discovered security vulnerabilities, rates each one by risk, and applies this to both commercial and custom software. Knowing which flaws matter most drives timely fixes.
controls.guidance: Review the vulnerability management procedure and the sources it monitors. Sample recent vulnerabilities to confirm they were assessed and assigned a risk rating.

controls.title: Inventory of custom software and components
controls.description: The organization keeps a list of its custom software and the third-party libraries and components built into it. A complete inventory makes it possible to react quickly when a component is found to be vulnerable.
controls.guidance: Obtain the software inventory or software bill of materials. Compare it against a sample of applications to confirm third-party components are listed accurately.

controls.title: Security patches applied on time
controls.description: Security patches are installed to fix known vulnerabilities, with critical patches applied within one month of release and others on a schedule set by the organization. Unpatched systems are a leading cause of breaches.
controls.guidance: Compare patch release dates with installation dates on a sample of systems. Review the patching policy and any records of exceptions or delays.

controls.title: Public web apps protected from attack
controls.description: Internet-facing web applications are protected either through regular vulnerability assessments, at least yearly and after changes, or through an automated attack-blocking solution. These applications face constant attack from the open internet.
controls.guidance: Review results from application security assessments, with dates, and confirm findings were fixed. Where an automated solution is used, inspect its configuration and confirm it is active.

controls.title: Automated protection for public web apps
controls.description: Internet-facing web applications sit behind an automated tool, such as a web application firewall, that continuously detects and blocks web attacks. Alerts from the tool are sent to staff who can respond.
controls.guidance: Inspect the web application firewall or similar tool configuration to confirm it is in blocking mode, kept current and generating audit logs. Verify alerts are investigated.

controls.title: Payment page scripts authorized and controlled
controls.description: Every script that runs in a customer's browser on a payment page is approved, checked for integrity, and listed with a reason it is needed. Rogue scripts are a common way attackers skim card data from checkout pages.
controls.guidance: Obtain the inventory of payment page scripts with business justifications. Review the integrity checks in use, such as content security policy or subresource integrity, and confirm approvals for each script.

controls.title: Production changes follow change control
controls.description: Changes to live systems go through a defined change process that records the reason, security impact, approval, testing and a back-out plan. Uncontrolled changes can open security gaps or break protections.
controls.guidance: Review the change management procedure. Sample recent production changes and confirm each has a documented reason, impact assessment, approval, test results and rollback plan.

controls.title: PCI controls confirmed after major changes
controls.description: After a significant change, the organization checks that all relevant PCI DSS controls are in place on new or modified systems and that documentation is updated. Big changes often introduce systems that miss required protections.
controls.guidance: Ask for a list of recent significant changes and the post-change verification records. Confirm that inventories, diagrams and other documents were updated to reflect each change.

controls.title: Test environments kept separate from production
controls.description: Development and test environments are kept apart from production and access controls enforce that separation. Less secure test systems should not offer a path into live systems.
controls.guidance: Review network diagrams and segmentation or access control settings between environments. Interview staff and observe how separation between pre-production and production is enforced.

controls.title: Separation of duties between test and production
controls.description: Duties for production and pre-production work are split so that only reviewed and approved changes reach live systems. This stops any one person from pushing unauthorized code into production.
controls.guidance: Review role assignments and deployment permissions. Interview staff and check pipeline settings to confirm developers cannot deploy unreviewed changes to production on their own.

controls.title: No live PANs in test environments
controls.description: Real primary account numbers are not used for development or testing unless the environment is fully in scope and protected like production. Test systems usually have weaker controls, so live card data there is easy to steal.
controls.guidance: Interview developers and testers about test data sources. Sample test databases or files to confirm they contain dummy or tokenized numbers rather than live PANs.

controls.title: Test data and accounts removed before go-live
controls.description: Test data and test accounts are deleted from systems before they move into production use. Leftover test accounts and data can give attackers an easy way in.
controls.guidance: Review the release checklist or procedure for removal of test artifacts. Sample production systems and applications to confirm no test accounts or test data remain.

families.name: Restrict Access to System Components and Cardholder Data by Business Need to Know

controls.title: Access control policies documented and in use
controls.description: Written policies and procedures govern how access to systems and cardholder data is restricted. They are kept current and known by the people who apply them, so access decisions stay consistent.
controls.guidance: Review the access control policies and procedures for currency and approval. Interview staff who grant or manage access to confirm they know and follow them.

controls.title: Access control roles assigned and understood
controls.description: Responsibilities for restricting and managing access have named owners who understand their role. Clear ownership keeps access reviews and approvals from being overlooked.
controls.guidance: Look for documented assignments of access management duties. Interview the people assigned to confirm they understand what they are responsible for.

controls.title: Access control model defined
controls.description: The organization has a defined model for granting access that reflects business and access needs, covers all system components and data, and gives each job function only the minimum privileges required. A clear model is the foundation for least privilege.
controls.guidance: Review the documented access control model, such as role definitions and the privilege matrix. Confirm it covers all in-scope components and ties privileges to job functions.

controls.title: Access granted by job role and least privilege
controls.description: Users, including privileged users, receive access based on their job classification and only the least privileges they need to do their work. Excess access increases the damage from a compromised or careless account.
controls.guidance: Sample user accounts and compare their access with their job roles and the access control model. Interview managers about how access needs are decided.

controls.title: Access privileges approved by authorized staff
controls.description: Any privileges granted to users require approval from people authorized to give it. Approval ensures access is deliberate and justified rather than handed out informally.
controls.guidance: Sample user access grants and check for documented approval from an authorized person. Compare the approver list against policy.

controls.title: User access reviewed every six months
controls.description: All user accounts and their privileges, including third-party and vendor accounts, are reviewed at least every six months to confirm they are still needed and correct. Problems found are fixed and management signs off on the review.
controls.guidance: Obtain the last two access review records. Confirm they covered all user and third-party accounts, that issues were remediated, and that management acknowledged the results.

controls.title: System and application accounts use least privilege
controls.description: Accounts used by systems and applications are given only the privileges they need to function, and only the specific systems or processes that depend on them may use them. Overpowered service accounts are a prime target for attackers.
controls.guidance: Review a sample of system and application accounts and their assigned privileges. Interview administrators about how required privileges were determined and limited.

controls.title: System and application account access reviewed
controls.description: Access held by system and application accounts is reviewed on a schedule set by targeted risk analysis. Issues are fixed and management confirms the access is still appropriate.
controls.guidance: Obtain the targeted risk analysis that sets the review interval and the most recent review records. Confirm reviews occurred on schedule, issues were addressed and management signed off.

controls.title: Direct queries of cardholder data restricted
controls.description: Users can reach stored cardholder data only through applications or controlled interfaces, and only administrators can query the underlying data stores directly. This limits who can pull bulk card data.
controls.guidance: Review database and data store permissions to identify who can run direct queries. Confirm ordinary users access stored cardholder data only through applications with defined roles.

controls.title: Access control systems enforce need to know
controls.description: Technical access control systems are in place on all system components to limit access based on each user's need to know. Policy alone is not enough; systems must enforce it.
controls.guidance: Review access control system settings, such as directory services and application role settings. Confirm all in-scope components are covered and that restrictions match need to know.

controls.title: Access systems enforce role-based privileges
controls.description: Access control systems are configured to apply the privileges defined for each person, application or system according to their job function. This keeps actual access aligned with what was approved.
controls.guidance: Inspect access control system configuration and compare assigned permissions for sampled accounts against role definitions. Confirm the system enforces those permissions.

controls.title: Access control defaults to deny
controls.description: Access control systems block everything by default and only allow what has been explicitly granted. This prevents new users or resources from gaining unintended access.
controls.guidance: Review access control system settings to confirm the default setting is deny. Test or observe that an account without assigned privileges cannot reach protected resources.

families.name: Identify Users and Authenticate Access to System Components

controls.title: Identity and authentication policies in use
controls.description: Written policies and procedures govern how users are identified and how they prove who they are. They are kept current and known by the people who rely on them, so authentication is handled the same way everywhere.
controls.guidance: Review the identification and authentication policies and procedures for currency and approval. Interview staff responsible for identity management to confirm they know and follow them.

controls.title: Identity management roles assigned and understood
controls.description: Responsibilities for user identification and authentication have named owners who know their duties. This keeps account management and authentication controls from being neglected.
controls.guidance: Look for documented assignment of identity and authentication responsibilities. Interview the people named to confirm they understand their duties.

controls.title: Unique ID for every user
controls.description: Each user gets their own individual ID before they can use system components or reach cardholder data. Unique IDs make every action traceable to a single person.
controls.guidance: Review user account lists from sampled systems for duplicate or generic IDs. Interview administrators about how IDs are issued and check audit logs to confirm actions are tied to individuals.

controls.title: Shared and generic accounts tightly limited
controls.description: Shared, group or generic accounts are used only when truly necessary, for a limited time and with documented justification and management approval. Even then, each user's identity must be confirmed before access so actions remain traceable.
controls.guidance: Identify any shared or generic accounts on sampled systems and request their business justification and approval. Check how individual users are verified before using them.

controls.title: Unique credentials for each customer environment
controls.description: This applies to service providers: staff who remotely access customer premises use different authentication credentials for each customer. A single compromised credential should not unlock many customers at once.
controls.guidance: Interview service provider staff and review remote access procedures. Sample customer environments to confirm credentials are distinct for each customer.

controls.title: User ID changes properly authorized
controls.description: Creating, removing and changing user IDs, credentials and related identity records is authorized and carried out only with appropriate approval. This prevents unauthorized accounts and privilege creep.
controls.guidance: Sample recent account creations, changes and deletions and match each to an approved request. Confirm the changes made match what was approved.

controls.title: Access removed promptly at termination
controls.description: When a user leaves the organization, their access is revoked right away. Former staff with live accounts are a significant insider and account takeover risk.
controls.guidance: Obtain a list of recent leavers from HR and compare it with active accounts across sampled systems. Confirm access was removed promptly and physical tokens were collected.

controls.title: Inactive accounts disabled within 90 days
controls.description: User accounts that have not been used for 90 days are removed or disabled. Dormant accounts often go unnoticed and are attractive to attackers.
controls.guidance: Review account lists with last login dates on sampled systems. Confirm no account has sat unused for more than 90 days while still enabled.

controls.title: Third-party remote access controlled
controls.description: Accounts that vendors and other third parties use to access, support or maintain systems remotely are enabled only when needed and switched off otherwise. Their use is monitored for unexpected activity.
controls.guidance: Review vendor remote access procedures and account status on sampled systems. Check logs showing when vendor accounts were enabled, used and disabled, and how activity is monitored.

controls.title: Idle sessions lock after 15 minutes
controls.description: Sessions left idle for more than 15 minutes require the user to authenticate again before continuing. This stops someone from using an unattended, logged-in workstation.
controls.guidance: Inspect system and application settings for session timeout or screen lock values. Test on a sample system that a session locks after 15 minutes of inactivity.

controls.title: Users authenticate with at least one factor
controls.description: Every user and administrator must prove who they are with something they know, have or are, such as a password, token or biometric. This confirms that the person using an ID is its rightful owner.
controls.guidance: Review authentication settings on sampled systems and observe a user signing in. Confirm each account requires at least one valid authentication factor.

controls.title: Credentials protected with strong cryptography
controls.description: Passwords and other authentication factors are made unreadable with strong cryptography when sent over networks and when stored. Stolen readable credentials give attackers direct access.
controls.guidance: Review vendor documentation and system configuration for how credentials are hashed and encrypted. Inspect credential stores and capture sample traffic to confirm nothing is in clear text.

controls.title: Identity verified before credential changes
controls.description: Before a password is reset or an authentication factor is changed, the user's identity is confirmed. Social engineering of help desks is a common way attackers take over accounts.
controls.guidance: Review help desk procedures for password resets and factor changes. Observe or interview staff to confirm they verify identity before acting on a request.

controls.title: Account lockout after failed login attempts
controls.description: An account locks after no more than 10 failed login attempts and stays locked for at least 30 minutes or until an administrator confirms the user's identity. This slows down password guessing attacks.
controls.guidance: Inspect lockout settings on sampled systems for threshold and duration. Test, where possible, that repeated wrong passwords trigger a lockout.

controls.title: Initial and reset passwords unique and temporary
controls.description: Passwords set for a new account or after a reset are unique to each user and must be changed at first login. Predictable or reused starter passwords are easy for attackers to guess.
controls.guidance: Review password setting procedures and system settings that force a change at first use. Observe or test a reset to confirm the temporary password is unique and must be changed.

controls.title: Minimum password length and complexity
controls.description: Passwords used as an authentication factor are at least 12 characters long, or 8 if a system cannot support 12, and include both letters and numbers. Longer, mixed passwords are much harder to crack.
controls.guidance: Inspect password policy settings on sampled systems and applications. Confirm length and character requirements meet the minimum, and document any systems limited to 8 characters.

controls.title: Recent passwords cannot be reused
controls.description: Users may not set a new password that matches any of their previous four. Blocking reuse stops users from cycling back to an old, possibly compromised password.
controls.guidance: Inspect password history settings on sampled systems. Test, where possible, that a recently used password is rejected.

controls.title: Authentication guidance shared with users
controls.description: Users receive clear guidance on choosing strong authentication factors, keeping them safe, not reusing old passwords, and changing them if they suspect compromise. Informed users protect their credentials better.
controls.guidance: Review the authentication policies and guidance materials given to users. Interview a sample of users to confirm they received and understand the guidance.

controls.title: Password-only access changed or monitored
controls.description: Where a password is the only factor for user access, it must be changed at least every 90 days, or the system must assess account security dynamically and grant access based on that assessment. This limits how long a stolen password stays useful.
controls.guidance: Identify systems where passwords are the only factor. Inspect expiry settings or the dynamic risk analysis configuration to confirm one of the two approaches is enforced.

controls.title: Password guidance for service provider customers
controls.description: This applies to service providers: where customers sign in with only a password, the provider gives customers guidance on changing passwords regularly and on what to do if a password may be compromised.
controls.guidance: Review customer-facing documentation, such as help pages or onboarding material. Confirm it explains periodic password changes and steps to take after a suspected compromise.

controls.title: Customer password-only access changed or monitored
controls.description: This applies to service providers: where customer accounts use a password as the only factor, those passwords must be changed at least every 90 days, or account security must be assessed dynamically to decide access. This limits exposure from stolen customer credentials.
controls.guidance: Inspect system settings for customer password expiry or dynamic risk analysis. Confirm one approach is enforced for all customer accounts that rely on passwords alone.

controls.title: Physical and logical tokens assigned to individuals
controls.description: Authentication factors such as hardware tokens, smart cards or certificates are issued to one user and never shared. Controls ensure only that user can use the factor.
controls.guidance: Review the token issuance procedures and assignment records. Interview users and observe how tokens are used to confirm they are not shared.

controls.title: MFA for administrative access into the CDE
controls.description: Administrators who access the CDE over a network, rather than at the console, must use MFA. Admin accounts are high-value targets, and a second factor stops attacks that rely on a stolen password.
controls.guidance: Inspect network and system authentication settings for non-console admin access. Observe an administrator connecting to confirm MFA is required.

controls.title: MFA for all access into the CDE
controls.description: Every user who accesses the CDE must use MFA, with narrow exceptions such as application accounts and phishing-resistant authentication. This blocks attackers who have obtained only one factor.
controls.guidance: Review authentication configuration for all paths into the CDE. Observe users connecting and confirm MFA is required for each type of access.

controls.title: MFA for remote access to the network
controls.description: All remote network access from outside the organization that could reach the CDE requires MFA, for staff, administrators and third parties alike. Remote access is a favorite entry point for attackers.
controls.guidance: Review VPN, remote desktop and other remote access configurations. Observe staff and third parties connecting remotely to confirm MFA is enforced.

controls.title: MFA systems configured to resist misuse
controls.description: MFA systems resist replay attacks, cannot be bypassed without documented management approval, use at least two different kinds of factors, and grant access only after every factor succeeds. Weak MFA setups give a false sense of security.
controls.guidance: Review vendor documentation and MFA system configuration. Interview administrators about any bypass options and observe logins to confirm all factors are checked before access.

controls.title: Interactive use of system accounts controlled
controls.description: If a system or application account can be used to log in interactively, that use is limited to exceptional cases, approved by management for a limited time, tied to a confirmed individual, and traceable to that person.
controls.guidance: Identify system and application accounts that allow interactive login. Review approvals, time limits and logs that link each use to a specific individual.

controls.title: No hardcoded passwords for system accounts
controls.description: Passwords and passphrases for system and application accounts that can log in interactively are not written into scripts, configuration files or source code. Hardcoded secrets are easily discovered and rarely changed.
controls.guidance: Interview developers and review a sample of scripts, configuration files and code repositories for embedded credentials. Look for use of a secrets vault or similar tool.

controls.title: System account passwords protected and rotated
controls.description: Passwords for system and application accounts are protected from misuse, changed on a schedule set by targeted risk analysis, and changed whenever compromise is suspected. They are also complex enough for how often they are changed.
controls.guidance: Obtain the targeted risk analysis that sets rotation frequency and complexity. Review password vault or rotation records to confirm passwords are changed on schedule.

families.name: Restrict Physical Access to Cardholder Data

controls.title: Physical security policies documented and in use
controls.description: The organization keeps written policies and procedures for physically protecting cardholder data, keeps them current, and makes sure the people affected know about them. Clear, shared rules are the foundation for every other physical safeguard.
controls.guidance: Review the physical security policy set and its last review date. Ask staff who handle facilities and media to explain where the procedures live and how they follow them.

controls.title: Physical security roles assigned and understood
controls.description: Someone is named as responsible for each physical security activity, and those people know what is expected of them. Without clear ownership, physical controls tend to drift or get skipped.
controls.guidance: Look for a RACI chart, job descriptions or a responsibility matrix covering physical security tasks. Interview the named owners to confirm they understand their duties.

controls.title: Facility entry controls restrict CDE access
controls.description: Doors and other entry points to locations housing systems in the CDE use controls such as badge readers or locks so that only approved people get in. This stops outsiders from simply walking up to equipment that processes card data.
controls.guidance: Walk the facility and observe how each entrance to rooms holding CDE systems is secured. Interview facilities staff about how entry is granted and revoked.

controls.title: Sensitive area entry monitored by camera or badge logs
controls.description: Entry into sensitive areas is tracked person by person using video, access control logs, or both, the monitoring is protected from tampering, and the records are kept at least three months. This lets the organization find out who was in a room when something went wrong.
controls.guidance: Inspect camera placement and badge reader coverage at sensitive area entrances. Confirm the recording or log system is protected from disabling and pull a sample of records to verify at least 90 days are available.

controls.title: Public network jacks restricted
controls.description: Network ports in places visitors can reach, such as lobbies or meeting rooms, are disabled or otherwise prevented from connecting to internal networks unless someone is authorized to use them. An open wall jack can give a stranger a direct path inside.
controls.guidance: Visit public and visitor areas and test or inspect network jacks. Review switch configurations or NAC settings showing those ports are disabled or limited to an isolated guest network.

controls.title: Wireless gear and network hardware physically secured
controls.description: Wireless access points, gateways, handheld devices, network and communication hardware, and telecom lines are kept where unauthorized people cannot reach them. Physical access to this equipment can let an attacker tap or reroute traffic.
controls.guidance: Observe where access points, switches, routers and telecom lines are located and how they are locked or mounted. Interview network staff about how this equipment is protected.

controls.title: Consoles in sensitive areas locked when unattended
controls.description: Admin consoles and terminals located in sensitive areas are locked so nobody can use them while they are left alone. An unlocked console is an easy way in for anyone passing by.
controls.guidance: Observe an unattended console in a sensitive area, or watch an administrator step away, and confirm the session locks. Check screen lock and timeout settings.

controls.title: Process for granting staff physical access
controls.description: There is a defined way to identify staff, approve their physical access, change it when roles change, and remove it when they leave, including returning or disabling badges. People should be easy to recognize and their access should match their current job.
controls.guidance: Review the documented procedure for issuing, changing and revoking staff badges. Observe how employees are visibly identified and check that changes to the badge system are limited to authorized administrators.

controls.title: Sensitive area access tied to job role
controls.description: Staff get into sensitive areas only when their job requires it, and that access ends right away when they leave or no longer need it, with keys and badges collected or disabled. This limits who can get close to critical systems.
controls.guidance: Compare the badge system's access list for sensitive areas against current staff roles. For a sample of recently departed employees, confirm their badges were deactivated and keys or cards returned.

controls.title: Visitor approval, escort and badge process
controls.description: Visitors to the CDE are approved before entry, escorted at all times, given a badge that looks different from employee badges and expires, and are clearly identifiable. This keeps guests from wandering into places they should not be.
controls.guidance: Review the visitor procedure, then observe a visitor arriving and moving through the facility. Inspect sample visitor badges to confirm they are visually distinct and have an expiration.

controls.title: Visitor badges returned or deactivated on exit
controls.description: When visitors leave or their badge expires, the badge is collected or switched off. A badge that keeps working after the visit can be reused by the wrong person.
controls.guidance: Observe visitors leaving and check that badges are handed back or disabled. Review the badge system for expired visitor credentials that remain active.

controls.title: Visitor log kept for at least three months
controls.description: A log records each visitor's name, the organization they represent, the date and time, and the staff member who authorized them, and it is kept for at least three months unless the law says otherwise. This gives an audit trail of everyone who came onsite.
controls.guidance: Inspect the paper or electronic visitor log for the required fields. Confirm entries go back at least 90 days and ask where older logs are stored.

controls.title: Media with cardholder data physically secured
controls.description: All media containing cardholder data, such as drives, tapes, backups or printouts, is kept physically secure. Loose media is one of the easiest ways for card data to walk out the door.
controls.guidance: Review procedures for protecting media and inspect storage rooms, safes or locked cabinets. Ask staff where media with card data is kept day to day.

controls.title: Offline backups stored in a secure location
controls.description: Backup media holding cardholder data that is kept offline is stored somewhere secure. Backups contain large volumes of data, so losing one can be as damaging as a system breach.
controls.guidance: Review the backup storage procedure and visit or obtain evidence about the storage site. Check logs or records showing backups are kept in the approved secure location.

controls.title: Offline backup site security reviewed yearly
controls.description: The security of each location holding offline backups with cardholder data is checked at least once a year. Conditions at a storage site can change, so periodic checks confirm it is still adequate.
controls.guidance: Ask for the most recent annual review of each backup storage location. Confirm the review covered physical security and that any issues found were addressed.

controls.title: Media classified by data sensitivity
controls.description: Every piece of media with cardholder data is labeled or categorized based on how sensitive its contents are. Classification tells people how carefully each item must be handled.
controls.guidance: Review the media classification scheme. Sample media logs or physical items to confirm each one has been assigned a classification.

controls.title: Offsite media shipments tracked and secured
controls.description: Any card data media shipped offsite is logged, sent by a secure courier or other trackable method, and its movement is recorded. This ensures nothing gets lost or diverted in transit.
controls.guidance: Review procedures for sending media offsite. Examine tracking logs and courier receipts for a sample of shipments to confirm each was logged and sent by a secure, trackable method.

controls.title: Management approval for media leaving the site
controls.description: Management signs off on all media with cardholder data before it leaves the facility, including media sent to individuals. This puts a deliberate checkpoint on data leaving the organization's control.
controls.guidance: Review the approval procedure. Pull a sample of offsite media log entries and confirm each one shows approval from an appropriate manager.

controls.title: Electronic media inventory logs maintained
controls.description: The organization keeps inventory logs of all electronic media that holds cardholder data. Knowing exactly what media exists is the only way to notice when something goes missing.
controls.guidance: Review the policy requiring an electronic media inventory, then inspect the current inventory logs for completeness.

controls.title: Electronic media inventory checked yearly
controls.description: The electronic media inventory is checked against what is actually on hand at least once a year. Regular reconciliation catches lost or stolen media.
controls.guidance: Ask for evidence of the most recent annual inventory reconciliation, such as a signed checklist or report. Confirm discrepancies were investigated.

controls.title: Paper records with card data destroyed securely
controls.description: Printed materials with cardholder data are shredded, pulped or burned once no longer needed, so the data cannot be pieced back together, and paper waiting for destruction is kept in locked containers. Discarded paperwork is a common source of card data leaks.
controls.guidance: Review the destruction policy and observe how paper is disposed of. Inspect the bins used for paper awaiting destruction to confirm they are locked, and review shredding vendor certificates if used.

controls.title: Electronic media destroyed or wiped when retired
controls.description: Electronic media holding cardholder data is physically destroyed or the data is made unrecoverable once it is no longer needed. Simply deleting files often leaves data that can be recovered.
controls.guidance: Review the media disposal policy and observe or obtain records of a disposal event. Look for certificates of destruction or secure wipe reports for a sample of retired media.

controls.title: Card-reading POI devices protected from tampering
controls.description: Devices that read cards by direct contact, such as payment terminals, are protected against tampering and unauthorized replacement. Criminals swap or alter terminals to skim card data at the point of sale.
controls.guidance: Review policies covering POI device protection, including inventory, inspection and staff training. Confirm the related sub-requirements are in place and followed.

controls.title: Up-to-date POI device list maintained
controls.description: The organization keeps a current list of its POI devices, including make and model, where each is located, and its serial number or other unique identifier. An accurate list makes it possible to spot a missing or substituted device.
controls.guidance: Examine the device list for the required details. Compare a sample of devices in the field against the list to confirm locations and serial numbers match.

controls.title: POI devices inspected for tampering or substitution
controls.description: Staff regularly inspect POI device surfaces for signs of tampering, such as added skimmers, and check that devices have not been swapped for fakes. Routine inspection catches skimming before many cards are compromised.
controls.guidance: Review the inspection procedure and the records of completed inspections. Interview staff who perform inspections and ask them to show what they look for.

controls.title: POI inspection frequency set by risk analysis
controls.description: How often POI devices are inspected is decided through the organization's targeted risk analysis. This ties inspection effort to the actual risk at each location.
controls.guidance: Obtain the targeted risk analysis that sets the inspection interval. Compare inspection records against that interval to confirm they happen as often as the analysis requires.

controls.title: Staff trained to spot POI device tampering
controls.description: People working around POI devices are trained to recognize tampering attempts, verify the identity of anyone claiming to be a repair technician, report suspicious behavior, and never install or replace devices without authorization. Frontline staff are the first line of defense against skimming schemes.
controls.guidance: Review training content and attendance records for staff in POI locations. Interview a sample of cashiers or store staff about what they would do if a technician arrived unannounced.

families.name: Log and Monitor All Access to System Components and Cardholder Data

controls.title: Logging and monitoring policies documented and in use
controls.description: The organization keeps written policies and procedures for logging and monitoring, keeps them current, and makes sure the people affected know about them. Consistent logging depends on clear, shared expectations.
controls.guidance: Review the logging and monitoring policies and their last review date. Ask staff responsible for logs to explain where the procedures are and how they apply them.

controls.title: Logging and monitoring roles assigned and understood
